title: Korach: not for heaven's sake (Avot 5:17)
hook: the Mishnah names Korach's quarrel as the dispute not for heaven's sake
tomorrow: Korach: Moses falls on his face

segments.voice: Yesterday, Korach said the whole congregation is holy, which is true, and used it to reach for power. Your line was what's under the argument. Did you catch a motive hiding under a good point? Day four hundred fifty-two.

Some arguments are over by Friday, and nobody remembers what they were about. Others go on for two thousand years, and people are still grateful for them. The Mishnah, in the collection called Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers, sorts every argument ever had into two piles. It gives each pile one famous example. For the good pile, two great teachers who disagreed about nearly everything. For the other pile, the rebel we met yesterday. Korach. Today: what makes an argument worth keeping.
screen: `SOME ARGUMENTS END BY FRIDAY.` → `SOME LAST TWO THOUSAND YEARS.` → `TWO PILES, TWO EXAMPLES.`

segments.voice: Here's the teaching, in paraphrase. Every dispute that is for the sake of heaven will in the end endure. Every dispute that is not for the sake of heaven will not endure. Which dispute was for the sake of heaven? The dispute of Hillel and Shammai. Which was not? The dispute of Korach and all his company. The Hebrew phrase is l'shem shamayim, for the name of heaven. It means an argument whose goal is the truth, not the person arguing. Hillel and Shammai founded rival schools around the turn of the common era, and their students argued over hundreds of questions of Jewish law. The Talmud says a heavenly voice finally declared that both schools speak the words of the living God, and that the law follows Hillel's school. The reason it gives is not that they were cleverer. They were patient and humble, they taught the other school's view along with their own, and they even mentioned Shammai's view first. Those arguments are still printed and studied today. That's what endure means. Now look at the other half of the line. It doesn't say the dispute of Korach and Moses. It says Korach and his company. Commentators have noticed this for centuries. Moses wasn't fighting for himself; he never wanted the job. And Korach's allies each wanted something different, so a fight that's about winning ends up turning on itself. Many teachers draw a simple test from this: in an argument for heaven's sake, you'd be glad if the other side turned out right, because then the truth won.
screen: `TWO PILES OF ARGUMENTS.` · `L'SHEM SHAMAYIM: FOR HEAVEN'S SAKE.` · `HILLEL AND SHAMMAI: STILL STUDIED.` · `KORACH AND HIS COMPANY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: argue for truth, not for winning. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one disagreement you're in right now, at home, at work, in a group chat. Ask it three quiet questions. What am I actually trying to find out? What's the strongest thing the other person has said? If they turned out to be right, could I live with that? You don't have to fix anything. Just notice which pile this argument belongs in today. Breathe slowly with it until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Korach. The rebel the Mishnah chose as its example of a dispute not for heaven's sake, set beside Hillel and Shammai, whose arguments endure.
Your line: not for heaven's sake. Today, before you push a point, ask yourself whether you want the truth or the win. Day four hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Pirkei Avot is studied a chapter at a time in many communities on Shabbat afternoons between Passover and Shavuot, and often through the summer, so this teaching about arguments comes around every year.

fork.setup: you're deep in an argument and suddenly realize the other person has a good point. what do you do?
options: change the subject before anyone notices.
say it out loud: that's a good point.
find a new argument so you still win.
fork.reveal: the Talmud praises Hillel's school for teaching Shammai's view, even mentioning it first. an argument for heaven's sake is glad when the truth shows up, whoever brings it.

original.note: Hebrew: for the sake of heaven, literally for the name of heaven.

trapdoor: what you thought: Korach was just a troublemaker who lost.
what it means: the Mishnah makes him the model of an argument that's about winning, not about truth.

what a scholar hears: Avot 5:17 pairs Hillel and Shammai with 'Korach and all his company', not 'Korach and Moses'; commentators read the missing name as a sign that Moses wasn't fighting for himself.

notes: Avot 5:17 numbering varies by edition (5:20 in some); confirm the reference used in the app.

Eruvin 13b: 'these and these are the words of the living God', halakha follows Beit Hillel because they were easygoing and humble, studied both views and mentioned Beit Shammai's first; confirm the paraphrase.
Dating Hillel and Shammai 'around the turn of the common era' is approximate; confirm.
The reading of 'Korach and his company' (not 'and Moses') follows later commentators (e.g. the Maharal and others); confirm attribution if a Keeper wants it named.
The 'would you be glad if they were right' test is presented as a teaching many draw from the Mishnah, not as the Mishnah's own words.
